job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Tomas Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Not much glamour. I wake up at seven because my father Pavel does, and he's loud in the kitchen. I apply to jobs until about noon, then I do the books for his tile shop in the afternoon, invoices and VAT, which is the only real accounting I do now. I studied accounting in Brno, finished in June near the top of my year, and did internships at a tax advisory firm and at a car parts distributor. I live at home, and I'd rather have my own place by next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine. Hype comes and goes, and I've seen enough of it. I'd tell my father the shop's invoicing will stay the same, and I'd tell friends to stop worrying about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel about the same as now. The hiring market is decent here, there are firms with openings, and nobody has called me back from three of the last five. That's the thing on my mind, not AI. I'd still like a proper desk and a proper salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new. Send out the CV, go to interviews, keep doing the shop's books. I'd follow up on the tax advisory firm in town, where my old supervisor said to check back in the autumn. I'd keep my savings where they are, they're in a plain account and I like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. A little tired of waiting, but okay. I'm a patient person, my father says too patient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the one pressure in your life right now that has nothing to do with AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The waiting. I did what was asked, I got good marks and good references, and I'm still on the kitchen chair at 23. My father says he started the shop at my age with a loan and a van, and I don't have a van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you would you talk to about the job search, and what would they say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father, who says to just start in any firm. My friend Radek, who got into a bank in Prague and tells me to move there. I don't want Prague. I want to stay near my family and take a normal job nearby.

say: I'd say hype comes and goes and the **invoicing** won't change.
I'd tell friends to **stop worrying** about it.
think: The real worry is **no callbacks** from three of my last five applications.
I still want a proper **desk** and salary.
do: Keep sending the **CV** and doing the shop's books.
Follow up with the **tax advisory firm** where my old supervisor said to check back.
feel: **Okay**, a little tired of waiting, and too patient, my father says.
S0.quote: I did what was asked, I got good marks and good references, and I'm still on the kitchen chair at 23.
fieldNote: His worry is the **slow search**, not AI.
Wants to stay near family and refuses to move to **Prague**, like his friend.
Compares himself to his father who started the shop at his age.

steps.text: Follow up with the local tax advisory firm in the autumn
Keep sending out the CV and going to interviews
Keep doing the tile shop's invoicing and VAT

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a normal change, like when spreadsheets arrived. People will adjust. At the same time I'd say firms shouldn't use it to cut every young person's job, and I'd say that to my father over dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the jobs I'm applying for are the ones that get hit. Entry-level accounting is data entry, reconciliations, checking invoices. If a program does that, a firm needs fewer of us. I'd be one of fewer, and I don't use any of the tools, so I'd have to catch up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd have to learn the tools, even if I don't like it. I'd ask the tax advisory firm what they use. I'd take a basic course at the chamber of commerce. And I'd apply to smaller firms, like my father's accountant, where a person still does the work. I'd still avoid risky moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm no good at this sort of thing, I like paper and a calculator. But I'm not a fool, and I know I must change at some point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which entry-level tasks in your field would go first, and what does that do to a job like the one you want?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The invoice checking and the data entry go first, I think. The firm where I interned had four juniors on that. They'd want two with the software. That's the part I'd have to compete for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend who graduated a year after you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn what the software does before they're asked. And to find a small firm where the boss still reads the books himself. At small firms the accountant is a person you trust, and trust is slower to automate.

say: I'd say it's a **normal change**, like when spreadsheets arrived.
I'd say firms shouldn't use it to cut **every young person's job**.
think: Entry-level accounting is **data entry and checking**, exactly what software takes.
I use none of the tools, so I'd have to **catch up**.
do: Ask the tax advisory firm which **tools** they use and take a basic course.
Apply to **small firms** where a person still does the work.
feel: **Anxious**: I like paper and a calculator, but I know I must change.
S1.quote: At small firms the accountant is a person you trust, and trust is slower to automate.
fieldNote: Sees his **junior-level tasks** as the first to go.
Reluctantly accepts he must learn the tools, but plans the slowest, safest route.
Places hope in small firms where trust matters.

steps.text: Ask the tax advisory firm which software they use
Take a basic software course at the chamber of commerce
Apply to small local accounting firms where people still do the work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nothing for a day, then I'd say we have to be sensible. Banks and governments shouldn't panic and shouldn't pretend. At home I'd say we keep the shop running, because tiles and walls stay real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be terrified. If the machine does all thinking work, a firm doesn't need an accountant at 23, or at 50. My whole degree points at the one kind of work that goes first. The only things left would be hands-on, and I don't have those skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop. My father's tile shop is real and physical, and I'd learn the trade, laying and ordering, alongside doing the books. I'd also put my savings in the safest place I can and stop spending on anything. I'd go to the labour office and ask what they offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel the floor going. I'm not a person who panics, but I'd be sleeping badly, no question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what changes about how you spend the next few months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The next two months would be about practical things. I'd take the hands-on work at the shop, and I'd ask a friend who's a plumber's son whether they need a bookkeeper. I'd count what I have, and I have enough for about a year if my parents help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your family the night this was confirmed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with my father and say we need a plan for the shop, because it might be the only steady thing. I'd say sorry that the degree might not be worth it. He'd say the degree isn't wasted, and I'd know he was trying to be kind.

say: I'd say governments **shouldn't panic** or pretend.
I'd tell my family we keep the **tile shop** running, because tiles and walls stay real.
think: If machines do all thinking work, a firm doesn't need an **accountant** at 23.
My degree points at the work that **goes first**.
do: Learn **tile laying and ordering** at my father's shop.
Move savings to the **safest account** and ask the labour office what's offered.
feel: **Alarmed**: I'd feel the floor going and sleep badly.
S2.quote: My whole degree points at the one kind of work that goes first.
fieldNote: Treats his degree as aimed at the **most exposed work**.
Turns to his father's tile shop as the hands-on fallback.
Calm voice hides the **alarm**; he admits he'd sleep badly.

steps.text: Learn tile laying and ordering at his father's shop
Move savings to the safest account and stop extra spending
Ask the labour office what retraining it offers
Plan with his father how the shop can keep running

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is not nothing, and people should use it. At home I'd say it's like the shop: you plan for the slow season. I'd mention it to my father's accountant, to see what she thinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I get a first job, and I need to treat it as temporary. I'd feel the ground shifting but I wouldn't be sure when. The risk is that I stay too long in the familiar thing, like I tend to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get the first job at a firm that does real client work. Learn the software on the job, whether I like it or not. Save more, maybe half of my pay, and take a part in the shop on weekends so I know the hands-on side. In two years I'd decide if I need a trade qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a manageable kind. There's time, which helps. The part I don't like is that I have to change my habits, and that's slow for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years of warning, what would you do differently from the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, I'd have no choice but to go straight to the shop. With five, I'd take the job and slowly learn. I'd also look at a plumbing or electrical course in the evening, like my cousin did, as insurance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd stop doing, or start doing, that you wouldn't if it were sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop thinking of accounting as a job for life. I'd think of it as a good start. And I'd take the evening course seriously, because it's the only way I'd be calm.

say: I'd say five years is **not nothing**, like planning for the slow season.
I'd ask my father's **accountant** what she thinks.
think: I'd get a first job but treat it as **temporary**.
My risk is staying too long in the **familiar**.
do: Take a firm with **real client work** and learn the software on the job.
Save **half of my pay** and work weekends at the shop.
feel: **Anxious**, but manageable: time helps, though changing habits is slow for me.
S3.quote: I'd stop thinking of accounting as a job for life. I'd think of it as a good start.
fieldNote: Five years let him **take the job** and plan a hands-on insurance.
Aware that his own **habits** are the risk.
Wants an evening trade course as backup.

steps.text: Take a first job at a firm with real client work
Learn the firm's software on the job
Start an evening electrical or plumbing course in year two

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a lot of time, so nobody should panic. I'd tell my father that the shop will probably still be there, and I'd keep it light. Some friends would say I'm in denial, and they might be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think I'm lucky. Ten years is a real career. I'd earn, save, maybe buy a flat in Brno by 28. But I'd still be afraid that I'd be too slow to see it coming, because I'm not the first to try a new thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get the job, earn the qualification as a chartered accountant, and watch what the senior people do. If the senior people are using the software and it works, I'd start using it too. I'd also buy a flat and keep saving, because that's practical in any world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others, but not calm. A decade is a long way off, but I know I'm a person who waits too long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you do with the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd mark a date in every year to review. It's like a service on a car. If it looks like the work is going, I'd change in good time. If not, I'd stay with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having a decade make you feel safe, or does it just push the worry further off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of both. It's safer than two years, but I'd be worried that I'd fall into the comfortable thing and ignore the warning. A decade can be a trap if you don't use it.

say: I'd say ten years is a lot of time so **nobody should panic**.
I'd keep it light with my father, who thinks the **shop** will last.
think: Ten years is a **real career**, but I might be too slow to see it coming.
I'm **not the first** to try anything new.
do: Qualify as a **chartered accountant** and watch what senior people do.
Buy a **flat in Brno** by 28 and keep saving.
feel: **Calmer** than the other pictures, but not calm: I know I wait too long.
S4.quote: A decade can be a trap if you don't use it.
fieldNote: The decade eases the panic but he **doubts himself**.
Plans an **annual review** like a car service.
Still anxious: he fears his slowness to change more than the date.

steps.text: Qualify as a chartered accountant while working
Review his career once a year like a car service
Save for a flat in Brno by age 28

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I have no hands-on skills, my degree is in the work that goes first, and I'd have no time. What would help is a plain plan from the government, a real retraining offer with a job at the end, and honesty from the firms about what they will automate and when. I'd take a trade course if I knew it led somewhere.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm slower to change than I should be, and I know it. I'd like someone to push me to try one of those tools this month, not next year.

headlineQuote: I'm slower to change than I should be, and I know it.
portrait: Tomas is 23, a **top graduate** in accounting from Brno who lives with his parents and keeps his father's tile shop books.
He is pragmatic, centre in his views, and prefers the **familiar**: he doesn't use AI tools.
His degree points at **entry-level** thinking work, which he fears goes first.
Moods rise from uneasy to **alarmed** in the 2028 world, where his only fallback is the tile shop.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because his degree and skills both point at work that goes first.
whatWouldHelp: A plain government plan, retraining that **ends in a job**, and honesty from firms about automation.
